Miranda: Isn't this a great place?
Janet: Yes, and it's classy. In fact, I've never heard of it.
Miranda: It's not new. Actually, I come here quite often. I was going to bring you here but never had a chance to.
Janet: There were so many things we were supposed to do together. In fact, going for a drink was one of them.
Miranda: I know, but you don't like to mix business with pleasure so ...
Janet: That's true, but today we're not here to talk business. Let's have a drink.
Miranda: Absolutely. It really will help you take your mind off things.

Janet: So, how did you come across this place?
Miranda: Actually, I used to do gigs here.
Janet: You were a musician? I didn't know. You're such a dark horse.
Miranda: I wasn't supposed to tell you. My career counsellor advised me not to. Of course, she thought that this information was going to jeopardize my chances of getting a better job.
Janet: What's the matter with that? It's obvious that the music and the fashion industry are closely connected to each other.
Miranda: I know. It was just a hobby but it was an arduous task. I was only supposed to play three times a week but ended up playing almost every night.

Janet: This is interesting. Thanks for sharing that with me.
Miranda: No problem. Of course I'm supposed to mind my own business, but what actually motivated you to sponsor five children?
Janet: I was just appalled by the situation in poor countries and wanted to help.
Miranda: Wow. You're so compassionate. I'm glad we work together.

Be Supposed To and Be Going To
You use the structure be supposed to and was/were going to when you want to talk about expectations, obligations or arrangements.
You can use be supposed to to talk about situations in the past, present or future.
subject + to be + supposed to + verb
Present: He is supposed to look into that today.
Past: He was supposed to look into that yesterday.
Future: He is supposed to look into that tomorrow.
You use be going to in the past to talk about something that was expected but did not happen. The sentence sometimes includes a "but" phrase to explain what happened.

The structure is:
subject + was/were going to + verb

Example:
I was going to bring you here but never had a chance to.
NOTE: When you say "supposed to", you link the /d/ and /t/ sounds together, Like this: be suppose_to
I was going to bring you here but never had a chance to.
There were so many things we were supposed to do together.
I wasn't supposed to tell you.
She thought that this information was going to jeopardize my chances of getting a better job.
I was only supposed to play three times a week but ended up playing almost every night.
Of course I'm supposed to mind my own business.
Using Expressions like “Of course” and “In fact”
You use expressions like of course, in fact, actually and really to emphasize that something is true.

To say that you agree or disagree with someone.
Of course, but has he broken any international laws?

To say something that you believe someone probably already knows or will not be surprised about.
Of course, there are justifications.

Using "in fact" and "actually"

To add something to what you have just said, especially something that may seem surprising.
In fact, these children start at the age of seven.
You also use phrases like “really”, “naturally” and “it is obvious” to emphasize that something is true.
In fact, I've never heard of it.
Actually, I come here quite often.
In fact, going for a drink was one of them.
Actually, I used to do gigs here.
It's obvious that the music and the fashion industry are closely connected to each other.
Of course I'm supposed to mind my own business, but what actually motivated you to sponsor five children?
